title: Kersey Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Kersey wells have a 48-foot median depth; see local yields, water levels, permit history, risks and drilling costs.
h1: What Kersey Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Kersey sits on the Weld County plains, where nearby well records show unusually shallow typical depths but a wide range of construction results. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records include 2,218 permitted wells, with 1,496 listed as constructed.

The local record points to a 48-foot median well depth, a 15.0-gpm median reported pump yield, and a median static water level of 8 feet below ground. Those figures are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a particular lot will produce. The permit, well construction, aquifer, and neighboring wells still matter.

sections.heading: Kersey well depth is usually shallow, but not always
sections.html:
The median reported depth near Kersey is 48 feet. The middle half of wells falls from 30 to 68 feet, and 90% are under 100 feet. That gives a driller a reasonable starting point for a bid on a typical plains property, rather than assuming a deep mountain-style hole.

The range is still wide. The deepest well in the records reaches 1,315 feet, while 8% fall between 100 and 300 feet and 2% between 300 and 600 feet. Local permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers for 1,563 wells, alluvial aquifers for 337, and Quaternary Alluvium for 46. Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 54%, so the exact formation beneath your parcel can change the plan.

sections.heading: Reported Kersey yields are strong, but verify the test
sections.html:
Only 271 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics describe tested wells rather than every permitted well. Among those reports, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 15.0 to 500.0 gallons per minute.

Seventy-six percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 20% fall between 5 and 15 gpm, and 4% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. No reported wells are under 1 gpm. For a buyer, that is encouraging, but a yield test and the approved permit use still control the practical water supply. An exempt household-use well is subject to the 35-gpm pumping limit, even when the aquifer could produce more.

sections.heading: Kersey water levels look shallower in newer records
sections.html:
Of the local records, 215 report a static water level. The median depth to water is 8 feet, with the middle half between 5 and 14 feet below the surface. That is important for excavation, casing, grout, pump placement, and protecting the wellhead from surface water.

The decade series does not suggest a dropping water table in these records. Median measured depth to water was 20 feet in the 2000s, 9 feet in the 2010s, and 7 feet in the 2020s. This is a record trend, not a guarantee for a specific parcel; measurement locations, seasons, pumping, and well construction can differ. Ask for the original static-water reading and compare nearby wells in Kersey, Garden City, and La Salle.

sections.heading: Kersey permits show steady drilling activity
sections.html:
Permit history shows wells being added across every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s. The largest recorded decade is the 2020s, with 401 permits, and the newest permit year is 2025. The records also include 264 permits from the 2000s and 205 from the 2010s.

The most frequently listed drillers are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 418 records; Clement, Glenn A., with 152; and R & R Well & Pump Inc. (Rank, Samuel C), with 84. These are names in the permit history, not a recommendation or a statement that they are available today. Before hiring anyone, confirm current licensing, insurance, scope, and who will handle the DWR permit and completion paperwork.

sections.heading: A typical Kersey well costs more than the drilled hole
sections.html:
The local cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 48-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,400 to $3,400. That is not the finished water system.

With a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the modeled finished-well range is about $8,400 to $15,400. A bid should identify casing, grout, pump size, pressure equipment, testing, electrical, trench length, access, and permit work. A shallow hole can still require substantial site and utility work. If a driller encounters different ground or the well must go deeper than the local median, the final price can move outside this planning range.

sections.heading: Check Kersey water quality, yield, and building constraints
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 2,356 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 12 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to test existing water and understand the parcel’s relationship to potential sources.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible despite the strong reported median. Review nearby completion reports, aquifer names, static levels, and pump tests before buying. Septic setbacks, wellhead protection, access for a rig, and separation from waste systems must fit the lot. A water-rights review is also important for irrigation or other uses; over-appropriated basins can require an augmentation plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Kersey, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Kersey is 48 feet. The middle half runs from 30 to 68 feet, and 90% are under 100 feet. Some wells are much deeper, including a 1,315-foot record. Your driller should review nearby construction reports because aquifer and ground conditions can change from one parcel to the next.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Kersey?
faq.a: At the local modeled rate of $50 to $70 per foot, a hole at the 48-foot median depth costs about $2,400 to $3,400 to drill. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,400 to $15,400. A deeper hole, difficult access, or different site work can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Kersey wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 271 local wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 500.0 gpm, and 76% report more than 15 gpm. These are reported test results, not a guarantee for an untested lot. Request the completion report and a current yield test before relying on the supply.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Kersey?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that a specific Kersey well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 2,356 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, along with 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well for relevant contaminants, review nearby land uses, and retest after construction, repairs, or a change in water quality.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Kersey?
faq.a: The recorded decade medians do not show a dropping trend. Median depth to static water was 20 feet in the 2000s, 9 feet in the 2010s, and 7 feet in the 2020s. Only 215 wells report static water levels, and measurements can vary by location, season, and pumping. Compare readings from nearby wells rather than treating the series as a guarantee.
